I am 69 years old and have farmed these 7 mu in Quzhou County for half a century. My father taught me, and now my hands know the soil better than any book. At my age, I do not chase new fads. I do what has put food on the table for three generations.

This autumn, I will sow winter wheat on all 7 mu. I will buy improved seed — likely Luyuan 502, the same kind most neighbors use, because it stands well against the spring wind here and gives steady grain. Before sowing, I will run the rotary tiller twice to break the maize stubble and level the field. For fertilizer, I will spread compound fertilizer as my basal dressing, then topdress with urea at jointing time when the wheat is hungry. In total, that comes to about 17 kg of nitrogen, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 5 kg of potassium per mu. I have a well, so I will irrigate three times: once before winter to help the seedlings survive the cold, once at jointing in spring, and once at grain filling to plump the heads. For pests and weeds, I will spray herbicide once after sowing, insecticide twice when aphids show up, and fungicide once if I see powdery mildew — four applications in total. I expect about 1,000 kg per mu if the spring rains cooperate.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will immediately sow summer maize. There is no time to waste — the season is short. I will use Denghai 605 hybrid seed, the same seed almost everyone in the village trusts. I will plant directly into the wheat stubble without tillage; the soil is already loose enough and the clock is ticking. For fertilizer, I will apply compound at sowing and maybe a side-dressing of urea at the big trumpet stage — about 16 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 4 kg potassium per mu. I will irrigate twice: once when the tassels emerge and once during grain filling. For chemicals, I will spray herbicide once and insecticide twice for armyworm and corn borer — three applications total. If the weather is fair, I should get around 1,100 kg per mu.

I keep my inputs modest because my land is small, my family is only three mouths, and I have learned that throwing more fertilizer at the crop does not always fill the grain sack. Water from the well is my insurance, and I use it carefully.
